questions.title: Site of action of thiazide diuretics
questions.question: The site of action of thiazide diuretics is:

options.C: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

explanations.A: Incorrect. The proximal convoluted tubule is where carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) act, not thiazides.
explanations.B: Correct. Thiazides act in the early DISTAL CONVOLUTED TUBULE, where they inhibit the Na+/Cl- cotransporter (NCC) on the luminal membrane, reducing sodium and chloride reabsorption and producing diuresis. This distal site also explains their enhancement of calcium reabsorption. It is the defining location of thiazide action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The thick ascending limb is the site of loop diuretics (furosemide), which block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The collecting tubule is where potassium-sparing diuretics (aldosterone antagonists, ENaC blockers) act.

questions.learning_objective: State that thiazides act in the distal convoluted tubule on the Na/Cl cotransporter.

questions.title: Diuretic to lower intracranial pressure in cerebral oedema
questions.question: Which of the following diuretics would be most useful to lower intracranial pressure in a comatose patient with brain injury and cerebral oedema?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Amiloride is a weak potassium-sparing diuretic and has no role in acutely reducing cerebral oedema.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ethacrynic acid is a loop diuretic; it reduces plasma volume but does not osmotically dehydrate the brain.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Furosemide can adjunctively lower intracranial pressure but is not the most useful single agent for cerebral oedema.
explanations.D: Correct. Mannitol is an OSMOTIC diuretic that is filtered but not reabsorbed; it raises plasma osmolality and draws water out of the brain across the intact blood-brain barrier, rapidly reducing cerebral oedema and intracranial pressure. This osmotic dehydration of the brain is why it is the agent of choice here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify mannitol (osmotic diuretic) as the drug to reduce cerebral oedema and intracranial pressure.

questions.title: Diuretic that decreases calcium excretion
questions.question: Which of the following diuretics decreases calcium excretion and could be used in idiopathic hypercalciuria and recurrent renal calcium stones?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Loop diuretics INCREASE calcium excretion (hypercalciuria) and are used in hypercalcaemia, the opposite of what is wanted for calcium stones.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing aldosterone antagonist without a useful calcium-retaining effect for stone prevention.
explanations.C: Correct. Thiazides such as hydrochlorothiazide enhance calcium REABSORPTION in the distal tubule, so they REDUCE urinary calcium. This hypocalciuric action makes them useful in idiopathic hypercalciuria to lower the risk of recurrent calcium stones. It is exactly the property asked for here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic and does not selectively reduce calcium excretion.

questions.learning_objective: State that thiazides reduce urinary calcium and are used to prevent calcium stones, unlike calcium-wasting loop diuretics.

questions.title: Potential side effect of thiazide diuretics
questions.question: Which of the following is a potential side effect of thiazide diuretics?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ototoxicity/deafness is a recognised adverse effect of LOOP diuretics (especially with rapid high-dose furosemide or ethacrynic acid), not thiazides.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Diarrhoea is not a characteristic thiazide effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cystitis is not a metabolic effect of thiazides.
explanations.D: Correct. Thiazides reduce renal urate excretion (they share the organic-acid secretory pathway and volume contraction enhances urate reabsorption), so they raise serum urate and can cause HYPERURICAEMIA and precipitate gout. This is a classic metabolic side effect, alongside hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia and hypercalcaemia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hyperuricaemia as a metabolic side effect of thiazide diuretics.

questions.title: How triamterene differs from spironolactone
questions.question: Although both spironolactone and triamterene are potassium-sparing diuretics, triamterene differs in that:

options.A: It has a greater natriuretic action
options.C: Its potassium-retaining action is not dependent on the presence of aldosterone
options.D: It acts from the luminal membrane side of the proximal tubular cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neither drug is strongly natriuretic; the potassium-sparing agents produce only mild sodium loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Anti-androgenic effects (gynaecomastia) are a feature of SPIRONOLACTONE, not triamterene.
explanations.C: Correct. Triamterene (like amiloride) blocks the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct DIRECTLY, so its potassium-sparing action does NOT require aldosterone. Spironolactone, by contrast, works only by antagonising the aldosterone receptor and so depends on aldosterone being present. This aldosterone-independence is the key difference.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Triamterene acts in the collecting duct, not from the proximal tubule luminal side.

questions.learning_objective: Contrast triamterene's aldosterone-independent ENaC block with spironolactone's aldosterone-receptor antagonism.

questions.title: Effect of low-dose dopamine infusion
questions.question: Dopamine used at a low infusion rate (2-3 micrograms/kg/min) is used to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dopamine does not slow the heart; at higher doses it tends to increase heart rate via beta-1 receptors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A pressor effect appears at HIGH doses through alpha-1 vasoconstriction, not at low renal-dose infusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased cardiac output is a mid-dose beta-1 effect, not the low-dose action.
explanations.D: Correct. At low doses (about 2-3 micrograms/kg/min) dopamine preferentially stimulates dopamine D1 receptors in the renal vasculature, causing renal (and splanchnic) vasodilation and INCREASING renal blood flow. This dose-dependent, receptor-specific effect is why low-dose dopamine is described as the renal dose.

questions.learning_objective: State that low-dose dopamine stimulates renal D1 receptors to increase renal blood flow.

questions.title: An action of furosemide
questions.question: Which of the following is an action of furosemide?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Furosemide increases calcium excretion and tends to cause HYPOcalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Furosemide is a potent diuretic; it has no antidiuretic effect.
explanations.C: Correct. By blocking the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, furosemide delivers more sodium to the distal nephron, driving increased potassium (and hydrogen) secretion, so it characteristically causes HYPOKALAEMIA (and a metabolic alkalosis). Potassium loss is a hallmark adverse effect of loop diuretics.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Loop diuretics increase magnesium excretion, causing HYPOmagnesaemia, not hypermagnesaemia.

questions.learning_objective: State that furosemide (loop diuretic) causes hypokalaemia and increased calcium/magnesium excretion.

questions.title: Diuretic that is an aldosterone antagonist
questions.question: Which of the following diuretics acts as an aldosterone antagonist?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Amiloride is potassium-sparing but blocks the epithelial sodium channel directly; it is not an aldosterone antagonist.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dorzolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used topically in glaucoma, not an aldosterone antagonist.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Triamterene is potassium-sparing via direct ENaC block, independent of aldosterone.
explanations.D: Correct. Spironolactone is a competitive antagonist at the mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) receptor in the collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. This receptor antagonism defines it as the aldosterone antagonist and underlies its use in hyperaldosteronism, heart failure and resistant hypertension.

questions.learning_objective: Identify spironolactone as the mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) receptor antagonist.

questions.title: Correct statement about thiazide diuretics (digitalis)
questions.question: Choose the CORRECT statement about thiazide diuretics:

options.A: They act in the proximal convoluted tubule
options.D: Caution is needed when combined with digitalis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thiazides act in the distal convoluted tubule, not the proximal tubule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thiazides RETAIN urate (causing hyperuricaemia); they are not uricosuric.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thiazides tend to reduce, not increase, renal blood flow.
explanations.D: Correct. Thiazides cause hypokalaemia, and low potassium markedly potentiates the toxicity of digitalis (digoxin) on the heart, predisposing to arrhythmias. For this reason thiazides must be used cautiously with digitalis, monitoring and replacing potassium. This clinically important interaction is the correct statement here.

questions.title: Incorrect statement about diuretics (carbonic anhydrase)
questions.question: Regarding diuretics, which of the following statements is INCORRECT?

options.A: Metolazone is effective as a diuretic even when GFR is below 20 mL/min
options.B: Furosemide is useful in emergency and severe cases of oedema
options.C: Spironolactone is a good choice to treat oedema due to hyperaldosteronism
options.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition leads to increased reabsorption of sodium bicarbonate

explanations.A: Correct statement (so not the answer). Metolazone, a thiazide-like agent, retains diuretic efficacy in significant renal impairment, unlike ordinary thiazides.
explanations.B: Correct statement (so not the answer). Intravenous furosemide acts rapidly and is used in emergencies such as acute pulmonary oedema.
explanations.C: Correct statement (so not the answer). Spironolactone directly opposes aldosterone, so it is ideal for oedema of hyperaldosteronism.
explanations.D: Correct answer. This statement is INCORRECT: inhibiting carbonic anhydrase (acetazolamide) DECREASES bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, so more sodium bicarbonate is EXCRETED, producing an alkaline diuresis and a metabolic acidosis. The claim of increased reabsorption is the reverse of the truth, making it the false statement.
